question: If $B(\text{adj } B) = \begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{3} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{1}{3}\end{bmatrix}$, then the value of $\det(B^{-1}) =$
explanation:
Step 1 Analyze the given matrix equation. We are provided a scalar matrix on the right hand side. We can factor out the common diagonal element to write the equation as $B(\text{adj } B) = \frac{1}{3}I$, where $I$ is the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix.

Step 2 Recall the fundamental theorem relating a matrix and its adjoint: for any square matrix $B$, $B(\text{adj } B) = |B|I$. By directly comparing this identity to our given equation, we conclude that the determinant $|B| = \frac{1}{3}$.

Step 3 Apply the determinant property of inverse matrices, which states that $\text{det}(B^{-1}) = \frac{1}{\text{det}(B)}$. Substituting our known value gives $\text{det}(B^{-1}) = \frac{1}{1/3} = 3$.
